Phloem. This is the vascular tissue that transports sugars, amino acids, and other organic compounds throughout the plant, distributing the products of photosynthesis everywhere the plant needs them. Unlike xylem, which works passively, phloem cells remain alive and require metabolic energy to actively move nutrients from sources, typically the leaves, to sinks like roots, growing tips, and storage organs.

Phloem is composed primarily of sieve-tube members, which are the conducting cells and remain living, and companion cells, which are smaller but metabolically active and support the sieve-tube members. The transport mechanism in phloem is active transport. Sugar is actively loaded into the phloem at source tissues, which creates an osmotic gradient that drives water inflow. This osmotic pressure propels bulk flow of sap toward the sinks where the sugar is being used or stored. This is fundamentally different from how xylem transport works passively.

One remarkable feature of phloem is that it's bidirectional. Sugars can flow both upward from leaves toward roots and downward from leaves to developing fruits or storage roots, depending on where the sources and sinks are located. Primary phloem is laid down during a plant's early growth, while in woody plants, secondary phloem is produced by the vascular cambium and accumulates on the outside as part of the bark.

Phloem is easily damaged by pests like aphids and scale insects that puncture it to feed on the sap. It's also vulnerable to girdling, which is removing a strip of bark, because that severs the phloem and starves the roots below of the sugars they need. The sieve-tube members consume ATP during their active transport of sugars, so phloem respiration is energetically demanding. It works in concert with xylem, the complementary vascular tissue, in every vascular plant, having evolved alongside xylem in pterophytes, the earliest vascular plants.
